Oral History
Interview with Paul L. Howard
by Patricia Willard and Buddy Collette
Reel 1

Washington, D. C.
May 8-9, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
Ms. Willard: This is April 26, 1978 and (unintelligible) with Paul Howard.
PROCEEDINGS
Hello, Paul. We're back again to do a little talking with you. This is Buddy Collette.
Yeah, Buddy, how are you?

Fine, but, you know, you've inspired me and many of us musicians, and at this point we'd like to know some of the beginnings of your career as a musician, where you started, where you came from, some of the things that led you to be the kind of man and musician you are, a man that we've admired -- all of us.
Well, Buddy, I can start from here. I was born in Steubenville, Ohio, and that was quite a long time ago.
Do you remember
What year?
The year? Oh, yeah, 1895.
What month?
The month? Let me see, now, I got to think. Oh, September.
What's the date?
September 20, 1895. I hope I didn't make a mistake on that, because I forget all the time. I have to keep asking my wife all the time when I was born.
So, now, when you started as a musician, did you study with a teacher from the beginning or were you one of those natural talented people who just picked it
Oh, no, I was fortunate to have an Italian teacher.
Did you start on piano or anything like that in the beginning?
No, I started on -- what did I start playing on? I happen to forget, now. It's been a long time. I played on -- oh, I can't remember.
Did you ever play piano as a young man?
Oh, yeah, sure, but not too much piano, because --
That wasn't the first instrument then.
No, my first instrument was a -- what do you call that?
Trumpet? (Coronet?)
Coronet, coronet, coronet.
And that's what you studied with the Italian teacher, huh?
An Italian teacher, yes. That's what I had.

So you had really, beginning, possibly more than a lot of the black musicians. What I've heard, a lot of the black musicians, possibly at that time and even later, didn't get a chance to get to the great teachers,

because of money or just depending on where they lived and everything like that. You understand, that they were unable to get to an A-1 teacher. From your father, is that right? Who set that up for you?
My grandfather.
Your grandfather. Because, like I said, a lot of them didn't have money (inaudible) musicians, they just had to get up as they would go.
Well, I didn't have any money, but when they started telling me just about how things are going, why, they got me started on the -- oh, what do you call that? What do you call that, Buddy?
How things are going with the music, you mean, or the lessons?
Yeah, with the music. When they got me started going, how things were going with the music, well, I naturally -- naturally gave me the right thing to hang onto.
The right studies?
Yeah, the right studies.
Well, in other words, you had to go through all the technical things, the tone studies, all the exercises.
I certainly did, yes.
The proper lessons. Yeah, well, I
I certainly did.
But then that was taking you more into the classical field, wasn't it, more into --

Yeah, going into the classical field, because of the way they were teaching me, you know. I had an Italian teacher and he was a (unintelligible). He was really something else. And you had to remember things that he told you.
I see. Do you remember his name?
Do you remember the name of your Italian teacher?
No, I don't. I can't remember his name. I'm sorry.
Was he playing with the symphony orchestra or was he a player also?
Yeah, he was a player.
So he was actually working in some band or doing some work while he was teaching you.
Yes.
So when did you get to saxophone? Was that pretty close to the same period? Because I remember you as a saxophone player.
Oh, yeah, you know, when I bought the saxophone, they give me the saxophone later on, when I got pretty good on the coronet -- yeah, now we're getting
somewhere.
Okay.
I had to bring up the cornet. I forgot --
That's a start, see, because I knew that was the beginning.
Yeah, that's the beginning. And then when I got the cornet, then I jumped onto -- boy, I got so I could play it real good, and played in churches and things like that.
Was there gospels at the time, or jazz or what-have-you? In the churches, what did you play, what kind of music?
What kind of music?
Or was it church music?
Oh, church music.
So what about -- at that period, did you do any jazz playing, like, say, when I was a young man in high school, we had a couple of jazz bands and things like that. Did you play anything like that?
No, we played nothing but the classics.
Oh, classics. So what about your move to, say, the Los Angeles area? About how old were you then, when you came to Los Angeles?
When I came to Los Angeles? I was
trying to think. Wait a minute. I'm trying to think, Buddy, how old I was. Let me see. Well, --
So why don't we go back to the coronet, and things that you can remember -- see, that's an instrument that --
Oh, yeah. The coronet --
-- the favorite (Inaudible) instrument to a lot of us.
Oh, yeah, well, it was a good one to me, and I had to play at a -- what do you call that, I had to -- kind of forget what -- oh, boy. Well, anyhow, I had the coronet.
Uh-huh. So you mentioned, too, or someone did, that your father was a coronetist?
Yeah, my father was a coronetist.
And did he play in some of the jazz bands, too?
Oh, no, he didn't play in the jazz bands. He played strictly classical music, and got mad at me because I wasn't playing it.
I see. Well, do you remember, when you came out to Los Angeles, how old you were?
Yes, I remember. When I got to Los Angeles, let's see, when I got to Los Angeles, Buddy, I was --
Do you think you were 20 years old, or younger?
Oh, I was 20, yeah.
You were about 20?
About 20, yeah.
So what was the main reason for coming out, to see what the musical abilities were, I mean, as far as working as a musician, or what?
No, to play the coronet.
To play the coronet, in Los Angeles?
Yeah, in Los Angeles.
Did you come out for a specific job?
No, I just come out to play, so I could play my horn.
Were there friends of your out here at the time?
No, nobody.
You didn't know any of the musicians?
No, no, nobody. Nobody but me.
What about some of the people you met at the time, who influenced you? Who was playing then? Do you remember any of those people?
No, I can't remember none of the names of any of them.
At that time.
At that time.
How about later?
Later? Well, I didn't get into -- Later, (inaudible) none
of them, because they didn't have nothing to do with you that much. You ever been around Italians?
Yes.
Well, --
You mean, that wasn't the creative jazz. But it seems like later on, you met jazz players.
Oh, yes, I met jazz players later on.
When was that, about, do you remember? I mean, who were some of the first jazz people you met?
Don't know none of remember the names. Can't remember any of the names.
What about Lionel Hampton?
I met him in -- it was about -- oh, he was -- it was quite a number of years after I -- later, yeah with Lionel.
I see.
Lionel didn't have anything. He didn't -- she's got it.
(Recording interruption)
Okay, the last question was about when you met Lionel or when he worked with you or when you worked with him. Do you remember some of those days?
Well, yes, he worked with me at the -- 1925. That's when he worked with me.
Was he playing vibes at that time, or just playing drums?
Playing drums.
Only drums, not vibes.
No, wasn't playing vibes. I don't remember whether he was playing vibes or not. I can't remember.
I had heard stories that he was mostly a drummer in the beginning.
It sounded like he played vibes later, but (inaudible)
Yeah.
Was it your band he joined, or you just happened to be playing --
It was my band.
And do you remember what club you were working in?
Wasn't working at a club, we were just playing -- practising at the -- oh, it was the Nightingale.
Why don't we let Mrs. Howard and Mr. Howard talk about it for a minute?
That's why you're here.
Okay, would you take the microphone? Mr. Howard gave Lionel And you said that Mr. Hampton --
Lionel his first job.
-- his first job.

He went to Long Beach and brought up a band. (See, Les Hite and Lionel, George Orendorff -- he's a trombone player (Inaudible) and Louis (inaudible)) on the circuit, and some woman, brought them out here. He was just a young boy,
see. And they were playing a date there in Long Beach. And Lionel got into a little trouble (inaudible).
That's fine, you're doing just fine.
You're giving us some good information,
yes.
That's right. You tell us the things you remember, and then you'll probably remind him of more things.

So at the time, George (Brendorff) was he told Paul about Lionel with Paul playing at the Nightingale. And (inaudible), and they were rehearsing at the time to go into this embassy. I forget the fellow's name that opened it, but that was one of the high class places (inaudible).
So it would be in Hollywood.
Yes, it was in Hollywood. And George and Paul went down to Long Beach, on a Sunday, and Lionel was they had Lionel (inaudible) in jail. He was arrested.
Yeah, I remember that. so they got him out and brought him back to the city and that's when Lionel joined Paul's band.
(inaudible) And Louis Taylor, do you know him?
No. Is that the trombone player?
Yeah.
He's a trombone player out of Chicago.
No, I didn't -- this group with (inaudible).
He was with (inaudible). And do who is that the Embassy you remember Quince Street that was on --
Embassy?
Yes. That's the -- we've got the picture of the (inaudible).
I don't remember.
You don't remember?
Uh-uh. But I know I played at the Embassy. Yeah. I can't remember the --
That's the first big band they had.
That was actually a big band, then.
Yes, it was.
Well, what about Lawrence Brown? Was he around at that time, or did he come later?
No, Lawrence was around at that time.
Lawrence is in that picture. So is Charlie. Charlie was on the piano.
Who would that be, Charlie?
Charlie? I don't remember who Charlie was.
He lives on the west side, and is a wonderful --
Isn't that -- not Charlie Lawrence, is it?
Yeah, Charlie Lawrence.
Charlie Lawrence, was that --
Yeah.
Charlie Lawrence, eh? How about that, yeah. Sure, I know Charlie Lawrence.
And Louis Taylor, George Ohrendorf, Lawrence Brown and Lionel. Who was on the tuba?
Tuba Jack. Tuba Jack.
He was using tuba at that time.
What Jack? Do you know his last name?
James Jackson.
James Jackson on tuba, uh-huh.
Yeah.
James Jackson.
You know Jack?
I think I've heard of him. I don't know him, though.
You forgot it.
Yeah. Okay, at that period, then, what about people like Alton Red? Did he come later?
Oh, he come later.
Much later, right?
Much later.
Who are some of the others you remember? Was -- what's that composer who wrote Harvey Brooks? Was he around at that period?
Piano, yeah.
I'm thinking of names, but I don't --
He played piano, you did it right.
Harvey Brooks?
(Inaudible) I may be mistaken then, because Harvey was on piano, instead of --
Harvey was, instead of Charlie Lawrence, okay.
Harvey
What about people like Coleman Hawkins? Was he ever in Los Angeles?
Yeah.
Not at that period?
Not at that period, but he played with another outfit there, down at -- down on --
He came out here with -- who was he playing with? And they played at the Cotton Club. Don't you know, when Sebastian was having guest bands? Coleman Hawkins was with Duke, wasn't he, or with --
No, uh-uh, it was somebody else.
Dope's -- Louis Armstrong.
He was with Louis Armstrong, do you think, at the time?
I was just trying to --
I don't know whether he was with Louis or not, but I'm not sure. I can't be sure of that. [No]
Now, I don't remember clearly, because--
But he played --
Hm?
He played at that place, because --
Yeah, at the Cotton Club.
Cotton Club, yeah.
Pops played at the Cotton Club. He came out two different times. With Armstrong.
Yes.
And (inaudible) Redman, what's his name?
Don Redman.
Don Redman's band played there, too. At that time, when they had guest bands, Paul's band would do the intermissions, and play for the shows.
Yeah.
Coleman Hawkins probably (inaudible) came out with Fletcher Henderson.
Right, right.
Fletcher Henderson, uh-huh. She sure got it, she got it down.
She got it, yeah, that's it.
That's it.
So did you ever get a chance to work with Coleman?
With Coleman?
with Coleman Hawkins, yes.
Oh, yes, got a chance to work with him lots of times.
When was that, when you worked with Coleman? Do you remember when?
No, I don't remember when. I can't remember none of them.
Do you know what year (Inaudible) about?
Oh, it was about -- what year are we doing now? What year are we in now?
This now is '78.
Oh, no, not now --
You mean, we're talking about?
But you mean what we're talking about, with Lionel? Was that '25, '26, with Lionel Hampton?
Yeah, somewhere around in there.
That when Coleman Hawkins came out and worked with him.
Yeah, '26 or '27. It had to be that late, because --
At what point did you name your band? Your band was known as Paul Howard's Quality Serenaders.
Paul Howard's Quality Serenaders, and before that I (Inaudible) the Blackbirds. Yeah.
And which --
I can hold it for you.
Good.
In what year -- do you remember what year it became known as the Blackbirds?
No, I don't remember what year. But it wasn't none of these years way down in here now.
It was later?
Later, way later.
You mean, the '30s?
Not the '30s, no, no.
Not the '30s?
No, no.

The Quality Serenaders, according to this book by Albert McCarthy, that was the name of your band during the '20s, but I don't know exactly when. It mentions that you recorded, though, in the '20s. Is that right?
Yeah, recorded in the '20s.
It said, I believe, the first time was with the Black and Tan Orchestra.
Uh-huh.
Was that your first recording.
That's it. Had to get the Black and Tan in there some kind of way.
Yeah, that's coming up.
Long time ago. Black and tan.
Do you remember -- okay.
Who led the Black and Tan? Who was the leader?
Harry Sutherland.
And you were part of that.
Uh-huh.
Who else was in that orchestra?
James Jackson, and -- what's -- Papa Mudson?
Papa Mutt?
Papa Mutt.
Mutt Carey, isn't it?
Yeah.
Carey, what's his name? Mutt Carey?
Yeah, Mutt Carey. And there was somebody else in that band. I can't think of the one.
Reb Spikes.
Reb Spikes? Was he in there?
No, uh-huh. Reb never played with us. He got mad.
And according to this, you left the Black and Tan Orchestra in 1923?
Says, to take a quartet known as the
Quality Four into a local cafe.
Yeah, that's true.
What cafe would that have been?
Hummingbird.
Hummingbird?
Yep, uh-huh, she's right.
Where was that located?
On 12th Street.
12th?
Between Central and the next street over, I think it was Gladys Avenue. Yeah, it was on 12th.
On 12th Street, between Central and Gladys Avenue.
Uh-huh.
And it said, under Harvey (inaudible) this group recorded six titles in 1924. Is that right?
Okay?
Yep.
Do you have any of those records?
I think I do have, I'm not sure.
That would be interesting to hear, and to know that the names -- you know what lable they were on? The name of the company?
Uh-uh, I don't remember what label it was on.
And what was -- who were the members of the quartet, Harvey Brooks and you and who else?
Let' see.
Leon Hærriford?
Leon Hærriford, yeah. Got to get him in there somewhere.
Tin Can Henry?
Tin Can Henry.
There you go, that's good.
That's great. What were the rest of his names?
Henry Allen.
Allen?
Uh-huh.
Another Henry Allen. And then, you added Thomas Valentine on banjo?
Uh-huh.
And became the Quality Serenaders.
Yep.
Is that right? So it must have been -- the Quality Serenaders must have been around '24, '25.
Easy.
And then it says here you went on tour with blues singer Hazel Meyers, but it ended in disaster in Amarillo, Texas a month or two later.
Yep.
What kind of disaster?
Well, we had to stop playing because they wouldn't --
They went broke?
They went broke, and the rain got us. It was raining, oh, boy.
So you had to disband everything?
Disband everything, come home. That was something, boy. I forget those things. Maybe Susie might remember them.
The Quality Four were the first Negroes that for Warner Brothers, when they first had their radio station, did a session on the radio.
How did that come about?
Well, it came about -- someone came down to the cafe, and heard them.
I forgot about it.
And (inaudible).
How about that? That's really -- yeah.
That's right. She had it. I forget all them things.
Well, you're remembering good, too.
Carolyn Snowden and myself, and a girl named Arlene Johnson, we were entertainers down there, and we
went to the studio.
And don't forget Sue Hoye.
Sue Hoye?
Yeah.
That's the name I went by.
No kidding.
Sue Hoye.
Oh, you've been mentioned before. I believe Lawrence Brown mentioned you. You sang, right?
And we were the first to sing over the Warner Brothers radio, when they first opened that station.
Would that have been KFWB? Was that the station?
Yeah, that's what it was, KFWB.
I guess it was. I guess it was.
So that would be about what year?

Oh, that was in '24, because we were still the Hummingbird -- see, we left the Hummingbirds in the first part of '25, because Dr. Nelson, who owned the Hummingbirds, he opened this cafe, the Nightingale, on Washington Boulevard. And that's when he sent for Paul and them, that's when the show broke up in Amarillo. And he sent for the band to come there and open a new show at the Cafe Nightingale. And he brought them back here.
Cut if off.
(Recording interrupted.)
Paul?
Yeah.

I just have a few more questions about what the union situation was at that time. Was it all nonunion when you started working with your bands, or what happened, for instance, when you really began to get into unions? I know later on you were a big part of forming the union. You were an official or something in Local 767. How did that all come about, can you tell me?
Well, yes. How did that come about?
Yeah, I mean, the union.
The union? Well, --
In the beginning it was probably nonunion, wasn't it, when you first --
Yeah, it was nonunion. But they soon got that straightened out. It didn't take long, because we were always pushing to do the right thing. And that was the right thing, to have a union band.
Was it the white union in -- Local 47, was that existing at the time?
Yes, it was existing, yeah.
Local 47 had already come out here?
Local 47 -- oh, no, no, no.
Oh, there was no union in Los
Angeles.
No, there was no union, no. All this came up after the union. The union came up after all this, that's what I should have said, yeah.
But then, the white union was formed and then you still as a black musician couldn't get into the white union, is that right?
Oh, we could get into it all right, but it took a little time.
Yes.
You couldn't just --
Couldn't just join?
Couldn't just jump up and join.
So what did you have to do, form your own union? Is that what happened, later on?

No, we didn't form our own union. What we did was try hard to take certain pieces out of the band and make it worthwhile, try to sell them a bill of goods. On everything that I tried to do, I tried to be a gentleman, scholar and everything. That's the only way I could figure it out.
But we had all the union men we could keep up together at that time. Keep together.
So, about what year, do you remember when you did form the Local 767? Do you remember when that
Oh, I had nothing to do with forming it.
Do you know who did at the time? Were there any names that you remember?
Local 767?
Yes, who helped form that?
No, I don't.

But then you became involved at what point, do you know, when -- all I remember when I was a young member and just getting in was that you were financial secretary and was more or less running the whole thing. You seemed to be the strong post of the whole union.
Well, I was, then. But I took mine from the outside and put it in the inside. Does that sound like anything to you?
That sounds good, yes. You took all your experience, the same as you had been doing as a musician.
Yes.
Being a leader in developing things.
That's it.

The one point was, did you just decide to run for an office in the union? How did that come about? You know, Here you are, a musician with a for the band, and all of a sudden, you're financial secretary of the black union. You just
decided --
Well, I don't know. I can't -- I have to think of it a little while, Buddy, and then I'll be able to tell you.

Okay. This is interesting, because we'd like to know -- we knew you were an outstanding leader and instrumentalist, and at the same time you were outstanding as a financial secretary and running the union and keeping it together.
If I have a chance to think on it a little while, it'll come to me and then I'll be able to tell you. And I'd rather tell you the truth than tell you a lie.
Yeah, yeah.
That's the truth. You know me better than that. Yeah.
(Laughter)
Yeah. Do you remember who was president in those times? Do any of those names come to you?
Yeah.
I knew people like Leo Davis and Press Johnson, but I didn't know much other than those.
Well, did you know Papa Mutt?
I knew who Papa Mutt was. Was he president for awhile, too?
No, he was a member.
Yes.
But he wasn't president, no.
I know who Papa Mutt was.
But he played --
--what's his name? I mean
But Press Johnson (inaudible) Carl Johnson, or that was his son?
That was his son.
What was the father's name? It was Johnson, but I --
Press Johnson. That's what they called him, just Press.
(Laughter)
And, naturally, Leo Davis I knew, he was a saxophone player.

And did you know -- there's one other person I want to know did you know real well. But he's not -- his name doesn't come to me right now, but it will in a few minutes. Now, if we'll shut this machine off for a minute, --
(Recording interrupted.)

No, I don't know him, but his name is in the book, here. Now, we were trying to find out who started the union, 767, the musicians union in Los Angeles, the black union. Now, you mentioned -- what was his name?
Well, we've mentioned Robinson, but Robinson didn't start it.
He didn't?
No, he --
Do you remember anybody else --? (Inaudible.)
No, I can't remember anybody else.
Robinson (unintelligible).
Wasn't he president at the time?
Uh-uh.
(Inaudible.) He was a businessman. He had some kind of a business there on --
He had a business.
Near 23rd, I believe.
Uh-huh.
You know, you used to go in the back and pay your dues.
I can't remember what he -- the only thing I know about him, he was just getting in there.
Who, Robinson?
Yeah.
I didn't know that -- this was in twenty -- (Inaudible.)
Because he had Marshall Royal, and his --
What about Marshall's uncle?
His father.
His father?
His father or the uncle, because they were all musicians.
They were all musicians.
Maybe there we've got a key.
Wasn't Mr. Royal one of the -- wasn't he president at the time?
Mr. Royal? No.
President of the local?
Uh-uh.
Mr. Marshall.
He wasn't president.
No?
Uh-uh. But he was secretary. That's what he was, secretary.
Oh.
He was secretary.
Marshall's father was secretary?
Yeah, was secretary.
The uncle was also a musician, though, wasn't he? I didn't know what his name was.

He had an uncle in the -- yeah. He was crippled, and that's one reason why he didn't do nothing, because he was crippled. He was something. Them things get away from me. I had to say that. I'm sorry to say that, but that's the way --
Oh, you've been doing very good. That's fine.
It's kind of hard.
Well, we will sort of hit some other
periods and we'll come back to that. And if you think of anything, we'll get it down.
Okay.
Thank you.
(Recording interrupted.)
Was it KNX you just said?
I believe it was KNX, a station there in the old Examiner building. At that time, it wasn't old. I think that's where they first started their radio station.
At Seventh and Broadway, right?
Yes.
Now, who was singing there? Can you mention their names?
I said, Roberta Heiseck and myself, or the both of us. We were there, they were playing at Vernon Country Club.
With The Quality --
Quality Serenaders.
Do you remember that all right?
Oh, sure, I remember it.
When you broadcast on the radio.
When we broadcast.
When did it happen more than once? Was it regular or was it one time?
Well, no. We broadcast, I believe, on
a Monday night, I think. I think it was (inaudible), because we were out there, I think, six weeks and we left there and went to Mike Lyman's, downtown at the Club Alabama, on Spring.
Is that where the Club Alabama was then?
That's --
On Spring Street?
Yes.
Yeah.
You see, the Alabama on Central had taken the name from the Alabama on Spring.
Oh, I didn't know about the other one. You didn't tell me about that.
I didn't know that. Which year was that?
Oh, that was in -- I believe that was in '26, if I'm not mistaken.
So that was the original Club Alabama. On Spring Street.
Yeah.
And that's where you were, too?
Oh, yeah, we worked there.
Yeah, I didn't know about that one.
I had everybody.
Well, tell us who. You remember some
of the names who worked there?
Yeah.
See, I always thought Central was the only Club Alabama in Los Angeles.
Oh, no.
No, huh? Well, who were some of the people, do you remember?
In the band?
Yeah, at the Club Alabama on Spring.
Same bands.
Same bands.
Same band, yeah, same people.
Now, were there mixed audiences at the time, black and white, coming in the club?
Oh, yeah.
No, it wasn't a mixed clientele. They could have, but they didn't.
Well, was it mainly all white or mainly black at the time, that would come in to hear you?
No, I -- Susie said no, but I seen white and black in there.

Well, they could come, but I don't remember seeing any colored. They could come, but those that did come, they come upstairs and sat on the balcony and talked and chatted with us, just (inaudible). See, and then when it
closed there, that's when the band went to the Cotton Club
See, that Abe Lyman's brother on that Alabama on Spring Street.
What was his name?
Abe Lyman. He had a band, remember?
Oh, Abe Lyman and Mike Lyman were brothers.
Right.
Oh. How long --

And at the time, Fancheon of Fancheon and Marko staged the reviews there at the Alabama, because she was married to one of the Lyman Brothers. She was one of the sisters, and she married -- what was his name? Simon.
Simon.
But she was Abe -- Mike Lyman's sister-in-law.
Yeah, (unintelligible), yeah, sister-in-law.
You know the dance team? Fancheon and Marko?
Yeah. How long was there a Club Alabama downtown?
Oh, a long time.
And how long did you work there?
How long did we -- oh, about two or three years.
Two or three years?
No, not that long.
Not that long? She says not that long.
No. It was about -- I guess we worked there about six weeks.
At the Club Alabama?
Right.
The one downtown.
See, we left out of Vernon Country Club and went to Club Alabama on Spring Street. And then we went from there to the Cotton Club.
Okay.
Same thing comes to your mind. All we can do is use just little ideas here and there, yeah. It doesn't have to be a work of art.
Was this before or after the Quality Serenaders played the Montmartre in Hollywood?
That's what (inaudible). That's the Momart. Yeah.
I saw a picture in that book that said the Momart.
Momart, right.
And I've heard of the Momart in Hollywood.
See, that's what I want to do because there's a lot of things they're leaving out.
